pages.text: "Fresh tomatoes! Sweet oranges! Beautiful cloth!" Nine-year-old Adom held her grandmother's hand as they entered the busy market in Kumasi. "Grandma, how do people remember the prices of so many things?" Grandma Akua laughed. "Some use notebooks. Some use calculators. And some have been doing business for so long that they can calculate faster than you can run!" Adom watched a woman arranging baskets of vegetables while speaking to three customers. "She looks like the queen of the market," Adom whispered. Grandma smiled. "Perhaps she is a leader in more ways than you know."

pages.text: The woman was Auntie Serwaa. When a trader discovered that her delivery had not arrived, Auntie Serwaa helped her contact the driver. When two customers disagreed over an order, she listened carefully to both sides. When an elderly trader struggled to carry a basket, she found someone to help. "Is Auntie Serwaa the richest person here?" Adom asked. "I do not know," Grandma replied. "But leadership is not measured only by money." Adom thought about that. Auntie Serwaa seemed to spend as much time solving problems as selling goods.

pages.text: That evening, Grandma showed Adom photographs of Ghanaian markets from earlier generations. "Women have played important roles in trade across Ghana for a very long time," she explained. "They have built businesses, supplied communities and supported families." "Did women also become leaders?" Adom asked. "Certainly. Ghanaian history includes women who exercised economic, political and community leadership. Their roles differed across societies and periods." Adom studied the photographs. "Then our history is not only about kings, chiefs and wars." "Exactly. History is also about farmers, traders, craftspeople and ordinary people whose work shaped communities."

pages.text: The next Saturday, Auntie Serwaa asked Adom to help with a simple calculation. A customer bought four baskets of oranges at GH₵15 each. "The total is GH₵60," Adom said. The customer handed over GH₵100. "How much change?" "GH₵40!" Auntie Serwaa counted the money carefully. "Good. Accurate records protect both the seller and the buyer." Then she showed Adom the notebook where she recorded sales and expenses. "Money entering a business is not automatically profit," she explained.

pages.text: One morning, a trader received a delivery of tomatoes. Some were fresh. Others were badly spoiled. "Mix them together," suggested another seller. "Customers may not notice." Auntie Serwaa shook her head. "That would be dishonest and could harm people." She helped the trader separate the spoiled tomatoes and contact the supplier. Adom watched quietly. Later she asked, "Does honesty always make business easy?" "No," Auntie Serwaa replied. "But trust is valuable, and customers deserve safe products and truthful information."

pages.text: Adom noticed that some traders struggled to keep records. Others needed better storage or help understanding mobile payments. She shared an idea with her teacher. "What if our class created simple record books and number charts for traders who wanted them?" The teacher helped the children design clear, easy-to-use examples. Auntie Serwaa welcomed the idea. "Young people can learn from experienced traders," she said, "and experienced traders can learn from young people."

pages.text: At school, Adom presented a display called The Women Who Help Build Ghana's Economy. It included photographs used with permission, interviews and examples of businesses run by women. One visitor asked, "Can women build companies that sell products around the world?" Adom stood tall. "Yes! But they need skills, opportunity, access to resources and support, just like other entrepreneurs." Her teacher smiled. "That is an excellent answer."

pages.text: The following weekend, Adom returned to the market. Auntie Serwaa handed her a small notebook. "For your ideas," she said. "Grandma," Adom whispered, "I finally understand why Auntie Serwaa is like a queen." "Tell me." "She does not need a golden crown. She helps people, makes decisions and builds trust." Grandma nodded. "And what will you become?" Adom opened her notebook. "Perhaps a businesswoman. Perhaps an inventor. Perhaps both."

activities.question: What made Auntie Serwaa a respected leader in the market?
options: She listened, solved problems, acted fairly and helped others.
She wore a golden crown and refused to speak to customers.
She charged customers without counting their change.
activities.explanation: Auntie Serwaa earned respect because she listened carefully, solved problems, acted fairly and helped others.

activities.question: Four baskets of oranges cost GH₵15 each. How much do they cost in total?
A customer pays GH₵100 for GH₵60 of goods. What is the change?
Why is sales revenue different from profit?
options: Expenses must be deducted to determine profit.
All money entering a business is pure profit.
Suppliers give goods to traders for free.
activities.explanation: Money entering a business is sales revenue; expenses must be deducted to determine profit.

activities.question: How do traders contribute to society?
options: Supplying goods, creating livelihoods and supporting community life
Hiding spoiled goods inside fresh baskets
Refusing to keep records of sales and expenses
activities.explanation: Traders contribute by supplying goods, creating livelihoods, and supporting trade and community life.

activities.question: What should a leader do when two people disagree?
options: Listen fairly, seek facts and work toward a reasonable solution.
Shout louder than everyone else without listening.
Pick a side immediately before hearing the facts.
activities.explanation: A good leader listens fairly to both sides, seeks the facts and works toward a reasonable solution.
